title: Benchmarking Agents for Proving Theorems in Quantum Algorithms and Quantum Information
authors: Lei Zhang, Yusheng Zhao, Yimeng Cao, Ranyiliu Chen, Mingrui Jing, Jizhe Lai, Ziao Tang, Jingu Xie, Hongshun Yao, Xuanqiang Zhao, Guocheng Zhen, Chengkai Zhu, Xin Wang
abstract: Formal verification is becoming increasingly practical for quantum computing, yet the ability of AI agents to construct machine-checkable proofs in this domain remains unmeasured. We introduce Lean-QuantumAlg-Bench and Lean-QIT-Bench, two Lean 4 benchmarks containing 36 and 40 theorem-completion tasks for quantum algorithms and quantum information theory, respectively. Every task compiles in a fixed environment and is evaluated by deterministic proof checking and targeted semantic review, with difficulty weights assigned before model execution. We evaluate four models-GPT-5.5, Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4-Pro, and MiniMax M3-within a common theorem-proving framework under two settings: a task-only baseline and library-augmented deduction (LAD), which additionally provides access to a verified domain library. The highest difficulty-weighted scores are 60.4 out of 100 on the quantum-algorithm benchmark and 59.6 out of 100 on the quantum-information benchmark. LAD improves both score and completion rate in all eight model-benchmark comparisons, with gains of up to 15.9 points, providing evidence that verified libraries can strengthen domain-specific proof agents. The results reveal recurring weaknesses of agentic proving in areas such as quantum simulation, quantum learning, quantum information measures, and entanglement theory. Monetary and wall-clock costs per score point also vary substantially across models, highlighting important capability-efficiency trade-offs. We expect these benchmarks to establish a reproducible baseline for developing more capable and reliable proof agents, and to pave the way toward self-evolving AI scientists for advancing quantum information science.
summary: The paper introduces standardized benchmarks (QAlg-Bench and QIT-Bench) to rigorously test how well large language models can formally prove theorems in quantum information science. By comparing performance with and without access to verified domain libraries (LAD), the authors quantify model strengths, showing that structured knowledge significantly improves proof generation capabilities.
main_problem: The primary goal is to measure the current capability of large AI agents (LLMs) to construct rigorous, machine-checkable proofs for theorems in quantum algorithms and quantum information theory.
main_result: Library-Augmented Deduction (LAD) significantly boosts performance across all tested models compared to baseline attempts, while revealing recurring weaknesses in areas like quantum simulation and entanglement theory.
method: The authors developed two formal benchmarks, Lean-QuantumAlg-Bench and Lean-QIT-Bench, consisting of theorem-completion tasks evaluated within the Lean 4 proof assistant environment.
model_or_system: The work evaluates four state-of-the-art LLMs (GPT-5.5, Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4-Pro, MiniMax M3) attempting to prove theorems concerning quantum algorithms and information theory concepts.
key_observables: Difficulty-weighted scores (e.g., 60.4/100 on QAlg-Bench), completion rates, economic cost ($	ext{USD}/	ext{score point}$), and time cost ($	ext{s}/	ext{score point}$).
important_parameters: The evaluation compares a task-only baseline against the Library-Augmented Deduction (LAD) setting, which provides access to verified domain libraries.
main_assumptions: The benchmarks assume that performance can be quantified by deterministic proof checking within a fixed Lean 4 environment, establishing a reproducible baseline for future AI development.

paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, details the construction of the two benchmarks (QAlg-Bench and QIT-Bench), describes the evaluation methodology (baseline vs. LAD), presents quantitative results comparing multiple LLMs across various metrics, and concludes by discussing implications for AI science.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the frontier of formal verification in quantum theory, providing a concrete, quantifiable measure of AI's current mathematical reasoning capabilities within the domain of quantum computation.

Solid, unhatched bars indicate the baseline condition, while dashed, diagonally hatched bars indicate LAD. Black N/A labels mark unavailable economic-cost values.
